cards.example: Adding paid advertisements or a premium subscription to your free AI newsletter to start making a profit.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A business model where a customer pays a recurring price at regular intervals to access a product or service.
cards.example: Paying $15 every month to use a premium SEO tool like Semrush.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The portion of a company's revenue that is expected to continue in the future, often from subscriptions.
cards.example: If you have 100 students paying you $50/month for coaching, you have $5,000 in monthly recurring revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The difference between revenue and the cost of goods sold (COGS), divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage.
cards.example: If you sell a racket for $100 and it cost you $40 to buy it, your gross margin is 60%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The actual profit after working expenses, taxes, and interest have been paid.
cards.example: The money left in your bank account at the end of the year after paying for your ads, software, and taxes.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A brief presentation, often created using PowerPoint or Canva, used to provide an audience with a quick overview of your business plan.
cards.example: Showing a 10-slide presentation to an investor to convince them to give you money for your new marketing app.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A short section at the beginning of a business document that summarizes a longer report or proposal.
cards.example: The first page of your 50-page marketing plan that gives the "too long; didn't read" (TL;DR) version.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Any person, group, or organization that has an interest or concern in a business or project.
cards.example: The CEO, the marketing team, and even the customers are all stakeholders in a new product launch.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A situation in which a product has become diffused within a market; the volume of a product in a market has reached its maximum.
cards.example: Trying to sell a new smartphone in a country where every single person already owns two of them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage change of a specific variable (like revenue or users) within a specific time period.
cards.example: If your newsletter grew from 1,000 to 1,200 subscribers in one month, your monthly growth rate is 20%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The core soul or characteristic of a brand; the emotional heart of the brand.
cards.example: Disney's brand essence is often described as "Magical."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A document that provides guidelines for the way your brand should look and sound to ensure consistency.
cards.example: A PDF that says "Always use this specific shade of green and never use emojis in our official emails."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A set of guidelines that governs the content produced by a brand to ensure quality and alignment with values.
cards.example: A rule stating that your newsletter will never promote gambling or low-quality AI tools.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A pre-packaged set of promotional materials that provide information about a person, company, or cause, distributed to members of the media.
cards.example: A folder on your website containing high-res photos of you and a one-page bio for journalists.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The purchase of advertising space from a media company (like television, radio, or websites).
cards.example: Negotiating with a big football blog to show your banner ads for the next month.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total number of ad spaces a publisher has available to sell to advertisers.
cards.example: A popular website knowing it has exactly 50,000 sidebar ad slots to sell every day.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The act of reaching out to individuals or organizations to build relationships or promote content.
cards.example: Sending 50 personalized emails to other marketing influencers to ask for a "shoutout" for your newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Writing and publishing an article on someone else's website or blog.
cards.example: Writing a post about "The Future of AI" for a famous marketing site to get a backlink to your own site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of getting other websites to link back to your website to improve your SEO authority.
cards.example: Asking a sports news site to link to your article about "Badminton Training Gear."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The number of searches for a particular keyword within a specific period (usually a month).
cards.example: Finding out that "AI marketing tools" is searched 50,000 times every month on Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The position of your website in the search engine results for a specific keyword.
cards.example: Being happy because your blog post is now #1 on Google for the search term "LinkedIn tips."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A free listing in search engine results that appears because it's relevant to the search terms, not because you paid.
cards.example: Your website showing up right under the ads when someone searches for "best marketing coach."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A short summary of an answer to a search query, displayed by Google at the very top of the results page.
cards.example: Searching "How to play badminton" and seeing a boxed paragraph at the top that explains the rules instantly.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Information boxes that appear on Google when you search for entities (people, places, organizations) that are in the Knowledge Graph.
cards.example: Searching for "Cristiano Ronaldo" and seeing the box on the right with his age, team, and biography.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An instance of an internet user visiting a particular page on a website.
cards.example: If one person refreshes your blog post 5 times, it counts as 5 page views.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A group of user interactions with your website that take place within a given time frame (usually 30 minutes).
cards.example: A user visiting your site, reading three articles, and leaving; all of that counts as one session.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A model that gives 100% of the credit for a conversion to the very last channel the user interacted with before buying.
cards.example: A user sees your ad on Meta, then LinkedIn, but then searches your name on Google and buys; Google Search gets all the credit.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A model that gives all the credit for a sale to the first marketing channel that brought the customer to your website.
cards.example: Crediting a Facebook ad for a sale that happened two weeks later after the user received three follow-up emails.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of measuring marketing effectiveness that considers all the touchpoints a user interacted with before converting.
cards.example: Giving 20% credit to a LinkedIn post, 30% to a webinar, and 50% to a final sales email for a single purchase.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Average Order Value. The average amount of money a customer spends every time they place an order on your website.
cards.example: If you made $1,000 from 10 orders today, your AOV is $100.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An estimate of how hard it is to rank on the first page of Google for a specific search term.
cards.example: Seeing that "Marketing" has a high difficulty score (90/100), while "AI marketing for coaches" is much easier (20/100).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method used by search engines to identify the relationship between terms and concepts in a piece of content.
cards.example: If your article mentions "racket," "shuttlecock," and "court," Google knows you are talking about badminton, not tennis.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customer Data Platform. Software that creates a persistent, unified customer database that is accessible to other systems.
cards.example: A system that combines a user's website behavior, email clicks, and past purchases into one single profile.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Conversion Rate Optimization. The systematic process of increasing the percentage of website visitors who take a specific action.
cards.example: Changing the color of a button and simplifying a form to see if more people sign up for your service.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of customers who continue to use a product or service over a given period of time.
cards.example: If 80 out of 100 newsletter subscribers stay with you for a full year, your annual retention rate is 80%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The period of time (days/weeks) after a user interacts with an ad during which a conversion can be credited to that ad.
cards.example: If your window is 7 days, a user who clicks your ad on Monday and buys on Sunday is counted; if they buy next Monday, they are not.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Account-Based Marketing. A strategic approach that focuses on specific high-value target accounts rather than broad marketing to everyone.
cards.example: Creating a personalized ad campaign specifically designed for the 10 decision-makers at Nike.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Social Selling Index. A metric created by LinkedIn to measure your brand's presence and your ability to sell on the platform.
cards.example: Checking your score (out of 100) to see if you are successfully finding the right people and building relationships on LinkedIn.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Dynamic Creative Optimization. A form of ad technology that uses data to automatically change elements of an ad (like headlines or images) in real-time.
cards.example: An ad showing a "winter jacket" if it's currently raining in the user's city, or a "t-shirt" if it's sunny.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Small steps a user takes on your website that indicate they are moving closer to a final purchase.
cards.example: A user watching a video, adding an item to their cart, or clicking on your "Contact" page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When a marketing channel helps lead a customer to a conversion, even if it wasn't the final click that made them buy.
cards.example: A user discovers you on LinkedIn (Assistant), but buys later through an email (Closer). LinkedIn gets an "Assisted Conversion" credit.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of visitors who leave your site from a specific page, after having visited other pages on your site.
cards.example: Noticing that 60% of people leave your site after reaching the "Thank You" page (which is normal).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A platform that acts as an intermediary between publishers (affiliates) and merchant brands to track sales and pay commissions.
cards.example: Joining a network like Awin or Amazon Associates to find products to promote on your blog and get paid.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The phase-out of third-party cookies by major browsers, which makes it harder for marketers to track users across different websites.
cards.example: Google Chrome removing support for cookies, forcing advertisers to find new ways to target their ads accurately.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Consent Management Platform. A tool used by websites to ask for user permission to collect and use their data (for GDPR compliance).
cards.example: The banner that appears when you visit a site asking you to "Accept" or "Reject" cookies.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A small alert on a website that shows real-time actions taken by other users to build trust and urgency.
cards.example: A little box in the corner that says "Théo from Paris just joined the newsletter 2 minutes ago."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A ratio that compares the lifetime value of a customer to the cost of acquiring them. It measures the long-term profitability of your marketing.
cards.example: If a customer brings in $300 over their lifetime and costs $100 to get, your ratio is 3:1, which is the industry gold standard.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The number of new users that each existing user generates. It measures how "viral" your product or content is.
cards.example: If every 10 people who join your newsletter invite 2 friends who also join, your viral coefficient is 0.2.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy for limiting network traffic by putting a cap on how often someone can repeat an action (like calling an API) within a certain timeframe.
cards.example: A tool allowing you to pull only 100 LinkedIn profiles per hour to prevent their servers from being overloaded.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An open-standard authorization protocol that allows third-party services to access user information without exposing passwords.
cards.example: Clicking "Login with LinkedIn" on a new marketing tool instead of creating a new username and password.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A digital certificate that authenticates a website's identity and enables an encrypted connection (HTTPS).
cards.example: The "padlock" icon in your browser that tells users their credit card info is safe on your e-commerce site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An HTTP status code indicating that the resource requested is no longer available and will not be available again.
cards.example: Telling Google that a specific page is permanently deleted so it stops trying to scan it and removes it from search results.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An HTTP status code indicating that the server is currently unable to handle the request, often due to maintenance or overloading.
cards.example: Your website showing this error for 10 minutes while you are updating your database.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A secondary navigation system that shows a user's location in a website or web application.
cards.example: The text at the top of a page that looks like: Home > Shop > Men > Football Boots.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A Core Web Vital metric that assesses a page's overall responsiveness to user interactions throughout the visit.
cards.example: Google measuring how long the screen takes to "react" after a user clicks a menu button on their phone.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: HTML attributes used to specify the language and geographical targeting of a webpage.
cards.example: Telling Google "This is the French version of my site for France, and this is the English version for the USA."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Storing parts of your website on a visitor's computer so they don't have to download them again on their next visit.
cards.example: A visitor's browser "remembering" your logo so it appears instantly the second time they visit your site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A geographically distributed group of servers that work together to provide fast delivery of internet content.
cards.example: A user in New York loading your images from a server in New York instead of waiting for them to travel from your main server in Paris.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The "phonebook" of the internet that translates human-friendly domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses.
cards.example: Connecting your new website "theo-marketing.com" to the actual computer server where your files are stored.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The automated purchase of ad inventory from a specific publisher with a fixed price and set of terms.
cards.example: Using software to buy 1 million ad views on a specific news site for a fixed price of $2,000.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing technique where a series of ads are shown to the same person in a specific order to tell a story.
cards.example: Ad 1 introduces your brand, Ad 2 shows a customer testimonial, and Ad 3 offers a 20% discount code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A way to identify a device based on its unique configuration (browser version, screen size, OS) without using cookies.
cards.example: Recognizing a returning visitor even if they have deleted their cookies or are using an ad-blocker.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical analysis technique used to estimate the impact of various marketing tactics on sales and then forecast future results.
cards.example: Analyzing 2 years of data to see how much of your sales growth was caused by LinkedIn vs. how much was caused by TV ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of coordinating various marketing activities across different channels to ensure a unified and consistent customer experience.
cards.example: Ensuring your Facebook ads stop showing to a user the exact moment they open your latest sales email.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of republishing your content on third-party websites to reach a broader audience and drive traffic back to your site.
cards.example: Allowing a major business news site to republish your LinkedIn article with a link back to your newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When a community or individuals take control of a brand's image and messaging, often in an unauthorized or unintended way.
cards.example: Users on TikTok creating a viral challenge with your product that you didn't plan, changing how people perceive your brand.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Dividing your market based on personality traits, values, attitudes, interests, and lifestyles.
cards.example: Targeting "high-achievers who value productivity" rather than just "people who work in marketing."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The large volume of advertising messages that the average consumer is exposed to daily, making it hard for any single ad to stand out.
cards.example: Your ad getting lost in a user's Instagram feed because they have already seen 50 other ads today.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The rate at which the value or effectiveness of a marketing asset (like an email list or social media post) decreases over time.
cards.example: Realizing that after 48 hours, almost nobody is seeing or clicking on your latest LinkedIn post anymore.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Metrics that look good on paper but don't necessarily correlate with business goals like revenue or growth.
cards.example: Celebrating having 1 million followers when 0% of them are actually buying your products.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Metrics that tie specific and repeatable actions to observed results, helping you make decisions.
cards.example: Tracking your "Checkout Completion Rate" because improving it directly results in more money.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A self-reinforcing system where the output of one cycle becomes the input for the next, creating sustainable growth.
cards.example: Users find your free AI tool -> they share their results on LinkedIn -> more users find your tool.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Product Qualified Lead. A lead who has used your product and performed actions that indicate they are ready to upgrade to a paid version.
cards.example: A user on your free plan who has invited 5 teammates and reached the storage limit.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique for testing a hypothesis in which multiple variables on a page are modified to determine which combination performs best.
cards.example: Testing 3 different headlines, 2 different images, and 2 different buttons all at the same time (12 combinations total).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of shoppers who add items to an online shopping cart but abandon it before completing the purchase.
cards.example: If 100 people add a racket to their cart but only 30 buy it, your cart abandonment rate is 70%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of customers who have made more than one purchase from your store compared to the total number of customers.
cards.example: Seeing that 40% of your buyers come back to buy more badminton shuttlecocks every month.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Gross Merchandise Value. The total value of merchandise sold over a given period of time through a customer-to-customer exchange site.
cards.example: An e-commerce platform announcing they processed $1 million in total sales this year, even if their own commission is only 10%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A ratio showing how many times a company has sold and replaced its inventory during a specific period.
cards.example: Calculating that you sell and restock your entire supply of sports jerseys 4 times per year.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The average number of times a customer makes a purchase from your business during a specific period.
cards.example: Tracking that your average customer buys a new pair of shoes once every 6 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The study of the time delay between a customer's first purchase and their subsequent purchases.
cards.example: Identifying that customers usually wait 45 days before re-ordering supplements, so you send a reminder on day 40.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A digital file (CSV, XML, or TXT) that contains a list of products and their attributes (titles, images, prices) to be synced with ad platforms.
cards.example: Uploading your Shopify product list to Google Merchant Center to run Shopping Ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A tool which helps you upload your store and product data to Google and make it available for Shopping ads and other Google services.
cards.example: Managing your product images and stock status so they appear correctly in Google search results.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Stock Keeping Unit. A unique code assigned to a product to identify it in an inventory system.
cards.example: Having different SKUs for the same shirt model in "Blue-Medium" and "Red-Large."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of pricing where the cost per unit decreases as the customer buys more quantity or moves to a higher level.
cards.example: Selling 1 box of balls for $20, but 5 boxes for $80 ($16 each).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of gradually gathering information about a lead by asking for only 1 or 2 new details each time they interact with a form.
cards.example: Asking for "Email" in the first form, and "Job Title" in the second form a week later.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An automated action (like an email) that is sent because a user performed a specific action on your website.
cards.example: Automatically sending a "Forgot something?" email 2 hours after a user leaves an item in their cart.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A pre-scheduled series of automated messages sent to a lead over time to move them closer to a purchase.
cards.example: A 5-day email course where one lesson is delivered automatically every morning at 8 AM.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A feature in automation that allows you to set different paths for users based on their actions or data.
cards.example: IF the user clicked the link in Email 1, THEN send Email 2. ELSE, send a different reminder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Software that streamlines, automates, and measures marketing tasks and workflows.
cards.example: Using tools like ActiveCampaign or HubSpot to manage your entire email and lead strategy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of enhancing existing data by adding more details from third-party sources.
cards.example: Using a tool to automatically find the "LinkedIn Profile" and "Company Size" of a lead who only gave their email.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of moving data from a central data warehouse into operational tools like CRMs or ad platforms.
cards.example: Sending advanced customer scores from your database back into Salesforce so the sales team can see them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A webpage where subscribers can choose what types of emails they want to receive and how often.
cards.example: Letting a user choose to receive "Daily AI News" but opt-out of "Promotional Offers."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of removing inactive or incorrect email addresses from your marketing database to improve performance.
cards.example: Deleting subscribers who haven't opened an email in over 6 months to avoid being marked as spam.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of gradually increasing the volume of emails sent from a new IP address to build a positive reputation with ISPs.
cards.example: Sending only 50 emails on day 1, 100 on day 2, and 500 on day 3 when starting a new server.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Brand Indicators for Message Identification. An email standard that displays your brand's logo next to your authenticated emails in the inbox.
cards.example: Your logo appearing as a small icon in the Gmail app when you send your weekly newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of limiting the number of emails sent to a single ISP (like Gmail) over a period of time to avoid being blocked.
cards.example: Your email tool sending your 50,000 emails slowly over 5 hours instead of all at once.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A request sent from one application to another to perform a task or retrieve data.
cards.example: Your website asking the PayPal API "Did this user successfully pay their $50 invoice?"

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An e-commerce architecture where the front-end (what the user sees) is separated from the back-end (the shop's engine).
cards.example: Using Shopify to manage products but building a completely custom, super-fast website using advanced code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Progressive Web App. A type of application software that is delivered through the web but feels like a mobile app.
cards.example: A website that you can "install" on your phone home screen and that works offline.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Enhanced search results in Google that show extra information like ratings, prices, or images.
cards.example: Seeing "4.8 stars" and "In stock" directly on the Google search page for a pair of shoes.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A process of evaluating the technical aspects of a website to identify and fix issues that could affect search engine rankings.
cards.example: Checking for broken links, slow pages, and duplicate content to make your site healthy for SEO.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: How many clicks it takes for a search engine bot to reach a specific page from the homepage.
cards.example: Ensuring your best articles are only 2 clicks away from the home page so Google finds them easily.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The value or "SEO juice" passed from one page of a website to another through internal links.
cards.example: Linking from your most popular blog post to a new service page to help it rank faster.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A group of interlinked web pages built around a single "pillar" page that covers a broad topic.
cards.example: A main page on "Digital Marketing" linked to specific articles on "SEO," "Ads," and "Email."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of optimizing content for themes and topics rather than just specific keywords.
cards.example: Writing an article that covers everything related to "football" (stadiums, rules, players) to show Google you are an expert.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A small tool on a website that displays real-time notifications of recent sales or signups to build trust.
cards.example: A notification saying "5 people are looking at this hotel right now" on a booking site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A pre-designed path of conversation that a chatbot uses to interact with a user and answer their questions.
cards.example: Designing a series of questions: "Are you a coach?" -> "Yes" -> "Do you need help with SEO or Ads?"

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The technical and strategic system used to track, reward, and encourage existing customers to refer new ones.
cards.example: Automatically generating a unique link for every customer that gives them $10 when a friend buys.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A targeted marketing effort to re-engage past customers who have stopped buying from you.
cards.example: Sending a "We miss you" email with a 30% discount to anyone who hasn't purchased in 6 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An automated sequence of actions triggered when a user shows signs that they might cancel their subscription.
cards.example: IF a user hasn't logged in for 10 days, THEN send an email with a helpful tutorial to get them back.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technology that allows senders to include interactive elements (like carousels or forms) directly inside an email.
cards.example: Letting a user choose their racket color and size directly inside the email without visiting the website.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of automatically assigning new leads to the correct sales or marketing team based on their data.
cards.example: Sending "Enterprise" leads to your senior sales team and "Small Business" leads to an automated nurture sequence.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Dividing your audience based on the explicit choices they made regarding what content they want to see.
cards.example: Only sending "Football News" to the group of people who selected football as their favorite sport.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A systematic error in thinking that occurs when people are processing and interpreting information in the world around them.
cards.example: Using the "Anchoring Bias" by showing a high original price next to a sale price to make the discount look even better.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological phenomenon where people have a difficult time making a decision when faced with too many options.
cards.example: Reducing the number of coaching packages from 10 to 3 to help customers choose and buy faster.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A phenomenon where consumers will tend to have a specific change in preference between two options when also presented with a third option that is "asymmetrically dominated."
cards.example: Offering a Small coffee for $3, a Large for $7, and a Medium for $6.50 so people feel the Large is the best deal.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological phenomenon stating that people remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed tasks.
cards.example: Using a progress bar in a survey that shows "80% complete" to encourage the user to finish the last few questions.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The tendency to attribute greater accuracy to the opinion of an authority figure and be more influenced by that opinion.
cards.example: Featuring a testimonial from a world-champion badminton player on your sales page to increase trust.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological phenomenon where people do something primarily because other people are doing it.
cards.example: Adding a "Best Seller" or "Most Popular" tag to one of your coaching programs.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The psychological trigger that makes people want what is difficult to obtain or limited in supply.
cards.example: Stating "Only 5 spots remaining for the September intake" to drive immediate sign-ups.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing tactic that encourages customers to act quickly by setting a time limit on an offer.
cards.example: A countdown timer on a landing page showing that the special price ends in 15 minutes.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique in which exposure to one stimulus influences the response to a subsequent stimulus, without conscious guidance.
cards.example: Using images of high-end offices and luxury cars on your site to prime users to expect high premium prices.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A cognitive bias where people decide on options based on whether the options are presented with positive or negative connotations.
cards.example: Describing a product as "90% fat-free" instead of "10% fat" to make it sound healthier.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological heuristic in which people judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end.
cards.example: Ensuring the last session of your coaching program is extremely high-value so the client leaves with a great final impression.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The tendency to favor one's own group over those who are not part of the group.
cards.example: Using specific badminton jargon in your ads so real players feel like "you are one of them."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The phenomenon where a person is reluctant to abandon a strategy or course of action because they have invested heavily in it, even if it is failing.
cards.example: A user continuing a course they don't like because they already paid for it, which you can use to encourage "completion badges."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Marketing that engages the consumers' senses and affects their perception, judgment, and behavior.
cards.example: Using high-quality "ASMR" style sound effects of a badminton racket hitting a shuttlecock in your video ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Purpose, Audience, Context, and Tone. A framework used to guide the creation of effective communication and content.
cards.example: Before writing a post, you define your Purpose (Sell), Audience (Badminton players), Context (LinkedIn), and Tone (Expert but friendly).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The phenomenon where a person becomes so immersed in a story that they lose track of the real world and are more likely to be persuaded.
cards.example: Writing a long-form sales letter that tells the story of your personal struggle to success so the reader feels "connected" to the result.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A style of copywriting that focuses on the positive outcomes for the customer rather than the technical features of the product.
cards.example: Saying "Save 5 hours a week" (Benefit) instead of "Fast automated reporting" (Feature).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The small bits of text on a website or app that guide the user, such as button labels, error messages, and form instructions.
cards.example: Changing a button from "Submit" to "Get My Free Guide Now" to increase clicks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The text within an advertisement that is designed to catch interest and persuade a potential customer to take action.
cards.example: The three lines of text people see on your Facebook ad before they click the "Learn More" button.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A proven structure for writing headlines that grab attention and encourage people to read more.
cards.example: "How to [Result] in [Time] without [Pain]" is a classic marketing headline formula.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A value that indicates how easy it is for a person to read and understand a piece of text (like the Flesch-Kincaid scale).
cards.example: Ensuring your blog post has a readability score of "Grade 8" so it's accessible to a wide audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A style of writing where the most important information is presented at the beginning, followed by supporting details.
cards.example: Putting the main "AI news of the day" at the very top of your newsletter before the deep-dive analysis.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The space between what a person knows and what they want to know, used in marketing to encourage clicks.
cards.example: A headline like "The one AI tool that saved me 10 hours last week (it's not ChatGPT)" creates a curiosity gap.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of addressing and resolving a potential customer's concerns or doubts about your product during the sales process.
cards.example: Adding an FAQ section to your site that explains why your premium price is worth the investment.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Setting prices primarily based on a consumer's perceived value of a product or service rather than the cost of production.
cards.example: Charging $5,000 for a marketing audit because it will save the client $50,000, even if it only takes you 5 hours to do.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A pricing/marketing strategy based on the theory that certain prices have a psychological impact.
cards.example: Pricing a product at $99 instead of $100 because it "feels" significantly cheaper to the human brain.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological pricing strategy that involves using prices that end in "9" or "99" to make them appear lower.
cards.example: Selling a badminton racket for $49.99 instead of $50.00.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of keeping the price of a product or service artificially high in order to encourage favorable (high-quality) perceptions among buyers.
cards.example: Charging $2,000 for a one-day workshop so people assume it must be the "best" training available.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An ad technology that automatically creates different versions of an ad based on the viewer's data (location, interests).
cards.example: An ad showing a "Paris" background to users in France and a "London" background to users in the UK.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Also known as "Ad Fatigue." When an audience sees an ad so many times that they stop paying attention to it or start resenting it.
cards.example: Seeing your CTR drop from 2% to 0.5% because you've been running the same image for 3 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of replacing old ad images, videos, or text with new versions to combat ad exhaustion.
cards.example: Changing the colors and the headline of your LinkedIn ad every two weeks to keep it fresh.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of displaying ads based on the specific content of the webpage the user is currently viewing.
cards.example: Showing an ad for your AI newsletter on an article about "The Best AI Trends of 2026."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An algorithmic process that finds new people who share similar characteristics to a group of your existing customers.
cards.example: Feeding a list of your 1,000 best buyers to Meta to find 2 million new people with similar interests and behaviors.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A group of people you specifically exclude from seeing your ads to avoid wasting money.
cards.example: Excluding people who have already purchased your course from seeing the "Buy Now" ads for that same course.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When two or more of your ad sets target the same audience, causing them to compete against each other.
cards.example: Targeting "Badminton Fans" in one ad set and "Sports Enthusiasts" in another, where many people belong to both groups.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A representation of the social relationships between people on a social media platform.
cards.example: LinkedIn knowing that you are connected to Théo, who is connected to 500 other marketing managers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The strategy of balancing how many people see an ad (Reach) with how many times they see it (Frequency).
cards.example: Deciding it's better to show an ad to 10,000 people twice each rather than 20,000 people only once.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A business model where a brand sells its products directly to the end customer through its own website, bypassing retailers.
cards.example: A badminton brand selling only through their official site instead of putting their rackets in general sports stores.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A form of marketing where you empower your happiest customers to promote your brand to their own networks.
cards.example: Giving your top students a "certified" badge they can share on their LinkedIn profiles to show off their skills.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A measure of how many new users are acquired through the referrals or actions of existing users.
cards.example: Launching a "Refer 3 friends and get a month free" campaign that doubles your subscriber count in a week.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A version of Google Tag Manager where the tracking code runs on a private server you own, rather than in the user's browser.
cards.example: Sending data from your website to your own server first to bypass ad-blockers before sending it to Facebook.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A central system that stores and manages data from many different sources for the purpose of analysis and reporting.
cards.example: Using Google BigQuery to store all your LinkedIn, Google Ads, and CRM data in one single place for deep analysis.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Extract, Transform, Load. The three-step process of pulling data from one system, cleaning/fixing it, and putting it into a database.
cards.example: Extracting raw sales data, transforming it to remove errors, and loading it into your dashboard tool.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A mathematical process that uses data and statistics to predict future outcomes and trends.
cards.example: Analyzing 2 years of data to predict which customers are 80% likely to cancel their subscription next month.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical technique that predicts the likelihood that a visitor or customer will perform a specific action.
cards.example: Identifying which of your newsletter readers have the highest "propensity" (probability) to buy your premium course.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A tool that connects your marketing data directly from your server to the platform (like Meta) instead of using browser cookies.
cards.example: Telling Meta exactly when a purchase happened on your server to ensure your ad tracking is 100% accurate.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A set of rules and processes that ensure a company's data is accurate, private, and used correctly.
cards.example: Creating a company policy that defines exactly who can see customer email addresses and how that data is stored.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A command in SQL used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.
cards.example: Joining your "Customers" table with your "Orders" table to see exactly what each specific person bought.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advanced way of using AI to look at millions of customer journeys and determine exactly which marketing channel deserves credit.
cards.example: Using an algorithm to discover that a "small" YouTube mention actually caused 40% of your final sales.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical method that uses historical data and "prior knowledge" to estimate the effectiveness of different marketing channels.
cards.example: Using math to prove that increasing your LinkedIn spend by 20% will result in a 5% increase in total revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of measuring the "true lift" of an ad by comparing a group that saw the ad to a "control group" that did not.
cards.example: Proving that your ads actually caused new sales, rather than just showing ads to people who would have bought anyway.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique used in incrementality testing where you "track" people who would have seen your ad but you don't actually show it to them.
cards.example: Comparing "ghost" viewers to real viewers to see exactly how much your ad changed their behavior.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A scientific experiment where users are randomly assigned to either a test group (sees an ad) or a control group (no ad).
cards.example: Splitting your audience in half to see if a 10% discount code actually increases profit or just reduces your margin.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A way of turning words or content into numbers (vectors) so an AI can understand the "meaning" and relationship between them.
cards.example: Using embeddings to find out that your articles about "AI coaching" are semantically similar to "Future of Work."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A network of entities (people, places, things) and how they are connected, used by search engines to understand the world.
cards.example: Google knowing that "Théo Pezet" is a "Marketing Coach" because of his social profiles and mentions across the web.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A branch of AI that helps computers understand, interpret, and generate human language.
cards.example: Using an NLP tool to analyze 5,000 customer reviews and automatically categorize them by "Sentiment" or "Topic."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A type of security key used in APIs to prove that the person or app making a request has permission to access the data.
cards.example: A secret code your tracking tool uses to "talk" to the LinkedIn API and download your latest lead data.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A system where you store your content in one place but use code (APIs) to display it on any website, app, or screen you want.
cards.example: Writing a blog post once and having it appear instantly on your website, your mobile app, and a digital billboard.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique that allows you to turn specific features of your website or app "on" or "off" for specific users without changing code.
cards.example: Testing a new "One-Click Checkout" for only 5% of your users to see if it works before giving it to everyone.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A math model that calculates the probability of a user moving from one marketing channel to the next to determine channel value.
cards.example: Discovering that if people see your LinkedIn post first, they are 3x more likely to eventually buy via email.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method from game theory used to fairly distribute credit for a conversion among all the marketing channels involved.
cards.example: Determining exactly how many "dollars" of a $100 sale should be attributed to SEO, Social, and Email.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The people, processes, and technology that power a marketing team and ensure everything is efficient and measurable.
cards.example: The person responsible for making sure the CRM, the Email tool, and the Website all share data correctly.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A complete review of all the software and tools a company uses to see what is working, what is wasted, and what is missing.
cards.example: Realizing you are paying for three different tools that all do the same thing and choosing only the best one.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The idea that data is subject to the laws and governance of the country in which it is physically located.
cards.example: Ensuring that your European customer data is stored on servers in Europe to follow GDPR rules.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A series of proposals by Google to create web standards that allow for advertising without using individual tracking (third-party cookies).
cards.example: Google Chrome grouping you into a "segment" of users interested in "badminton" instead of tracking your specific name.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A cryptographic method where one party can prove to another that they know a value, without actually revealing the value itself.
cards.example: Proving to a website that you are over 18 years old without actually sharing your birthday or ID.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Advanced AI that analyzes the "mood" and specific meaning of a webpage to place relevant ads without using personal data.
cards.example: An AI realizing an article is about "healthy recipes" and placing an ad for organic olive oil.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The design and structure of every single interaction a customer has with a brand across all digital and physical channels.
cards.example: Mapping out how a user goes from a LinkedIn post to a webinar, then to a call, then to a "Thank You" gift.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A research method that collects and analyzes everything customers are saying about a brand to understand their needs and expectations.
cards.example: Reading support tickets, social media comments, and survey results to find the top 3 problems your customers have.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A metric used to measure how much effort a customer had to exert to get an issue resolved or a task completed.
cards.example: Asking a user: "On a scale of 1-7, how easy was it to book your coaching session today?"

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual graph that shows what percentage of a specific group of users (a cohort) continues to use a product over time.
cards.example: Seeing that users who joined in January leave after 2 months, but users who joined in February stay for 6 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using machine learning to estimate exactly how much money a specific new customer will spend with you in the future.
cards.example: Your system flagging a new lead as "High Value" because they behave like your best past customers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual map that shows how different types of data (like Customers, Orders, and Products) are related to each other in a database.
cards.example: A diagram showing that one "Customer" can have many "Orders," but each "Order" belongs to only one "Customer."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A new type of data storage that combines the flexibility of raw data (Data Lake) with the organization of a structured database (Data Warehouse).
cards.example: Using one system to store raw video files and structured sales tables at the same time for your AI to analyze.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A machine learning technique that trains an algorithm across multiple decentralized devices or servers without exchanging the raw data.
cards.example: An AI learning how people use an app on their phones without ever seeing the private data of those people.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advanced A/B testing method where the system automatically sends more traffic to the "winning" version while the test is still running.
cards.example: If Headline A is performing much better than Headline B, the system starts showing Headline A to 90% of people automatically.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical method used to find "hidden" groups or segments within a larger population based on their behavior.
cards.example: Discovering that you have a segment of "Silent Fans" who read every email but never click or comment.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of simplifying complex data sets by reducing the number of variables, while still keeping the most important information.
cards.example: Turning 50 different customer metrics into 3 simple "scores" to make it easier to understand their behavior.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique used by APIs to divide a large set of data into smaller, manageable "pages" so the system doesn't crash.
cards.example: Downloading your first 100 leads, then asking the API for the "next page" to get the next 100.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Running an experiment where the different versions of a page are chosen by your server before the website is even sent to the user.
cards.example: Testing two different pricing models where the user never sees the "flicker" of the page changing in their browser.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using complex math formulas (Calculated Fields) and data blending to create interactive marketing dashboards.
cards.example: Combining your Facebook spend and Google spend into one single "Total Marketing Cost" metric in your report.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using code (like Python) to automatically find and analyze thousands of search terms to find new content ideas.
cards.example: Running a script that finds all the "How to..." questions people are asking about badminton on Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A way of representing knowledge in the form of "Subject-Predicate-Object" so computers can understand relationships.
cards.example: "Théo (Subject) - teaches (Predicate) - Marketing (Object)."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The automated process of extracting data from websites for research or competitive analysis.
cards.example: Using a tool to automatically gather all the prices of rackets from 10 different competitor websites every day.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The direct revenues and costs of a business model expressed on a per-unit basis (per customer).
cards.example: Calculating that for every 1 euro spent on ads, you generate 4 euros in immediate revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The cost to acquire the next additional customer. It helps determine if you can afford to scale your budget further.
cards.example: Realizing that while your average CAC is 20, getting more customers now costs 45 each because you exhausted your best audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A branch of statistics that helps determine if a marketing action actually caused a specific result, rather than a coincidence.
cards.example: Proving that a celebrity post actually caused a sales spike, rather than the spike happening because it was a holiday.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical technique that calculates the effect of a campaign by comparing changes over time between a test group and a control group.
cards.example: Launching ads in Paris but not in Lyon, then comparing the growth difference between the two cities.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A predictive modeling technique that identifies which specific customers will only buy if they receive a marketing message.
cards.example: Targeting only persuadable users with a discount, instead of wasting money on people who were going to buy anyway.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of linking multiple identifiers like email and device ID from various platforms to a single, unique customer profile.
cards.example: Recognizing that the person who clicked an ad on a phone is the same person who just logged into your site on a laptop.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of linking user identities based on high-probability patterns like IP address and location rather than a 100% certain ID.
cards.example: Assuming two devices belong to the same person because they are always in the same house and use the same browser.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Linking user identities using 100% certain data, like a hashed email address or a unique login ID.
cards.example: Connecting a user's behavior across devices because they logged into their account on both their phone and computer.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A privacy proposal that allows browsers to show relevant ads without letting advertisers track individual users.
cards.example: Your browser remembering you liked sports gear and letting an ad auction happen locally on your device for privacy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Sophisticated Invalid Traffic. Ad fraud generated by bots designed to look exactly like real human behavior.
cards.example: A bot net that watches videos and clicks buttons on a schedule to steal your budget without being detected.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy to ensure ads appear in contexts that specifically align with a brand's values, going beyond simple safety.
cards.example: A luxury brand refusing to show ads on cheap discount sites, even if they are safe, to protect its premium image.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advertising business set up by a retailer that allows brands to show ads to shoppers on the retailer's own site.
cards.example: A racket brand paying a major online store to show their ad at the top of the search results for badminton.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A metric that measures the percentage of all Google searches for a specific category that go to your brand.
cards.example: If there are 10,000 searches for marketing coach and 2,000 are for your name, your Share of Search is 20%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A principle stating that the more choices a user has, the longer it will take them to make a decision.
cards.example: Limiting your website navigation to 4 items instead of 12 to help visitors find what they need faster.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A model predicting that the time to move to a target depends on the distance to and the size of the target.
cards.example: Making your Buy Now button huge and placing it where the user's thumb naturally rests on a screen.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of examining raw files from a web server to see how search engine bots and users interact with a site.
cards.example: Reading logs to discover that Google is wasting time scanning old, useless pages instead of your new blog posts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A server setup where you intercept requests to modify content like SEO tags before it reaches the user or Google.
cards.example: Using a tool to add technical SEO data to a website that is normally very difficult for developers to change.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Moving data processing closer to the user to reduce latency and allow for instant personalization.
cards.example: A website that instantly changes its language to French based on the user's city before the page even finishes loading.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy where a company builds its tech by connecting specialized tools via APIs rather than using one all-in-one suite.
cards.example: Using one specific tool for email, another for CRM, and another for data, making them all talk to each other.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A framework that allows data analysts to transform, test, and document data in a data warehouse using SQL.
cards.example: Using dbt to automatically clean your raw ad data and turn it into a perfect report every morning.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual map that shows the entire lifecycle of a piece of data, from its source to its final location in a dashboard.
cards.example: Being able to prove exactly where a Sale number came from before it reached the CEO's final report.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A search method that uses AI to find results based on meaning and intent rather than just matching exact keywords.
cards.example: A user searches for marketing help for people who hate selling and your site finds Empathy-based growth using AI.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy that uses AI to determine the most effective marketing action to take for a specific user at that exact moment.
cards.example: The system deciding that for User A, the best move is a video, but for User B, it's a 10% discount code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A separate, secure storage system where all sensitive customer data is kept, isolated from the rest of the tech stack.
cards.example: Keeping real names in a vault and giving the marketing team only fake IDs to analyze behavior safely.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A mathematical system for sharing information about a group while withholding information about individuals.
cards.example: A platform telling you 1,000 people liked your ad while adding noise so you can't identify any single person.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A data mining technique used to find purchase patterns by identifying which products are frequently bought together.
cards.example: Discovering that people who buy rackets also buy grip tape 85% of the time, so you create a bundle offer.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A score assigned to each customer that predicts how likely they are to stop using your service in the near future.
cards.example: Your CRM flagging a user who hasn't opened your last 3 emails as High Churn Risk to trigger a reminder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Marketing Return on Assets. A metric that measures marketing efficiency relative to total assets like brand equity.
cards.example: Measuring how much the value of your brand name has grown after a year of high-quality LinkedIn posting.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A system that tracks a lead from the first click through the entire sales process to the final dollar spent.
cards.example: Your CRM telling Google Ads: That person who clicked your ad 3 months ago just signed a 10,000 euro contract today.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advanced A/B testing method where an algorithm automatically shifts traffic to the winner in real-time.
cards.example: Starting a test 50/50, but as Headline A wins, the system automatically starts showing it to 90% of visitors.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A set of structured data that helps search engines understand the relationships between different entities on your site.
cards.example: Adding code that tells Google: This person is the Author of this Article and the Founder of this Company.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An SEO issue where search engines are confused about which version of a page is the master copy.
cards.example: Having two versions of your homepage active, causing Google to split your SEO power between them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Files like CSS or JS that prevent a webpage from appearing on the screen until they are fully downloaded.
cards.example: A user seeing a white screen for 4 seconds because a heavy script is loading before the main headline.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A performance metric measuring the time from when the page starts loading to when any content is rendered on screen.
cards.example: Ensuring the background and logo of your site appear in less than 1 second to make it feel fast.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total amount of time a web page is blocked from responding to user input, like clicks.
cards.example: A user tries to click Sign up but nothing happens for 2 seconds because the site is still processing code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An error where short windows make low-funnel ads look more effective than they actually are.
cards.example: Thinking search ads are your best channel because they get the last click, ignoring the months of branding work.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical method used to evaluate a marketing change by creating a fake version of the test group using other data.
cards.example: Using data from five cities to create a Synthetic Lyon to see how your ads changed the real Lyon.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A modern approach that uses time-series data to predict what would have happened if a campaign never launched.
cards.example: Proving that your Summer Sale caused 5,000 euros in extra sales that would not have happened naturally.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of automating the movement and synchronization of customer data across dozens of different tools.
cards.example: Ensuring that when a user unsubscribes from email, they are also removed from your Facebook ad audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A data platform that does not store data itself but instead sits on top of your existing data warehouse.
cards.example: Using your main database to power your marketing emails directly, ensuring data is always 100% accurate.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy where the ability for a tool to talk to other tools is built first, before the user interface.
cards.example: Choosing a tool because it can easily send data to your custom dashboard, rather than just for its looks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An architecture where software is built as a collection of independent services that communicate with each other.
cards.example: Having a Rating Service and a Cart Service working together independently to power an e-commerce site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A plan focused on getting users to voluntarily share their personal preferences and intent data.
cards.example: Running a Style Quiz where users tell you exactly which colors they like so you can personalize emails.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The return on ad spend calculated only on the additional sales generated by increasing your budget, rather than total sales.
cards.example: Spending 1,000 euros more to see if it actually brings in new customers or just the ones who would have bought anyway.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total marketing spend divided by the total number of new customers acquired across all channels, paid and organic.
cards.example: Combining your LinkedIn ad spend and your organic content costs to find the true average cost of a new student.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A SaaS metric stating that a company's combined growth rate and profit margin should exceed 40%.
cards.example: If your coaching business grows 30% per year and has a 15% profit margin, your score is 45, which is excellent.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When the expansion revenue from existing customers (upgrades) is greater than the revenue lost from customers who cancel.
cards.example: Losing 2 clients but having 5 others upgrade to your VIP program, resulting in more money than before.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A financial report that explains the changes in Annual Recurring Revenue from one period to another (New, Expansion, Churn).
cards.example: A chart showing the Board exactly why your revenue moved from 1M to 1.2M this year.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A SaaS efficiency metric that measures how much new revenue is generated for every dollar spent on sales and marketing.
cards.example: If your Magic Number is 1.0, it means every euro spent on ads creates exactly one euro of new recurring revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A measure of efficiency that shows how much venture capital a startup is "burning" to generate each dollar of new ARR.
cards.example: Spending 2M euros to get 1M euros in new revenue means your Burn Multiple is 2.0.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A single metric used to predict the likelihood of a customer renewing or churning based on their product usage and engagement.
cards.example: Assigning a Green score to a student who watches every video and a Red score to one who hasn't logged in for 3 weeks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical model used in marketing to predict the probability of a binary outcome, like "Will they buy or not?"
cards.example: Analyzing 50 different user traits to calculate that a 25-year-old male from Bordeaux has a 75% chance of purchasing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A data technique used to reduce the number of variables in a dataset while keeping the most important information for segmentation.
cards.example: Turning 20 different behavior metrics into 3 simple scores to identify your most profitable "Super Users."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A machine learning method that uses many "decision trees" to provide highly accurate predictions for lead scoring or churn.
cards.example: A system that looks at thousands of past paths to predict with 95% accuracy which leads will sign a contract today.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of building a network of entities and relationships on your site to help Google understand you as a brand authority.
cards.example: Linking your name, your company, and your specific coaching topics using structured data to get a Google Knowledge Panel.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. A system that connects an AI like ChatGPT to your private company data to give accurate answers.
cards.example: Creating a bot for your site that only answers questions using your past 200 LinkedIn posts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A system where AI "agents" are given goals and can use tools, plan steps, and complete complex marketing tasks autonomously.
cards.example: An AI agent that notices a drop in sales, analyzes the data, creates 3 new ad variations, and submits them for your approval.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A secure environment where two companies can match their data (like a brand and a publisher) without seeing each other's private info.
cards.example: Matching your customer list with a big news site's list to see which of your buyers also read that specific news site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A Google proposal to replace cookies by grouping users into broad "interests" (Topics) stored locally in the browser.
cards.example: Google Chrome telling an advertiser you are into "Sports" and "Marketing" without sharing your specific browsing history.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of content on a webpage or social media feed that is composed of advertisements.
cards.example: Noticing that Instagram shows 1 ad for every 3 organic posts, giving it an ad load of 25%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of buying advertising space at a low price and reselling it (or using it for high-value leads) at a higher price.
